name: Cuemath
line: Cuemath teaches in live classes with one tutor. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Cuemath: Cuemath teaches in live classes with one tutor, after an evaluation. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Cuemath's unit is the live class: after an evaluation, one tutor teaches a learner by video, usually twice a week, and decides what comes next [1][6]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after, right or wrong, updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem. Cuemath starts with a MathFit Evaluation of about 65 minutes with a specialist, then matches the learner with a tutor [6]. After that, progress is tracked through the tutor's assessments [4].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Cuemath the unit is the class: a live video session with one tutor, usually twice a week, with worksheets between classes [1][4][5]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [12].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. An answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. In Cuemath the tutor decides what comes next, following the learner's school curriculum and goals [6]. Progress reports highlight concept mastery, and we found no stated rule for what counts as mastered [4]. AMP's rule is open source: open to peer review and contribution.

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. In Cuemath, homework revises past topics alongside current chapters, and practice mixes topics based on past performance [4]. We found no review schedule in the pages we read [4][5]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [11].

rows.range: Kindergarten through grade 8, then Algebra 1 and 2, Geometry, Precalculus, AP Precalculus and AP Calculus, with test prep [5][1].
rows.start: A MathFit Evaluation of about 65 minutes with a specialist, then a match with one tutor [6].
rows.teaching: A live tutor teaches one learner by video, with a shared whiteboard and on-screen manipulatives [5][6].
rows.next: The tutor decides, following the learner's school curriculum and goals [6]. Practice mixes topics based on past performance [4].
rows.mastery: Tracked through the tutor's assessments. Progress reports highlight concept mastery. We found no stated rule for what counts as mastered [4].
rows.review: Homework revises past topics, and practice mixes topics [4]. We found no review schedule in the pages we read [4][5].
rows.adult: Books class times and keeps a computer with video ready [1][4]. The tutor plans and teaches [6].
rows.reports: Session feedback and progress reports in a parent app, and parent-teacher meetings [4][5].
rows.evidence: No outcome study found on its site, and no entry in Evidence for ESSA or the What Works Clearinghouse as of November 2026 [7][8].

theirs: Cuemath is an online math tutoring company. This page is about its live one-to-one classes in the United States [2]. Cuemath says its classes are taught by a live tutor, not by AI or recorded video [1].

A learner starts with a MathFit Evaluation of about 65 minutes, then is matched with one tutor who teaches every class [1][6]. Classes are live video on Cuemath's own platform, with a whiteboard and manipulatives [5][6]. Most learners in kindergarten to grade 8 meet twice a week, and high schoolers three times [1]. The tutor follows the learner's school curriculum and goals [6] and adapts lessons in real time [4]. Between classes come homework that revises past topics and practice that mixes topics [4].
credit: A live tutor who teaches one learner and stays the same from class to class [6].
Tutors pass a math test, a teaching assessment and training before they teach [6].
Tutoring as a method has strong evidence in randomized trials [10].

theirs: We found no study on Cuemath's site that compares its students' math learning with similar students who did not use it. We found no Cuemath entry in Evidence for ESSA or in the What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports as of November 2026 [7][8].

Cuemath's impact page credits it with a 24% gain in reasoning skills and gives no sample, comparison group or method [3]. A paper that Cuemath's own pages link to is a 2023 randomized trial of 742 tutors on a virtual tutoring platform. It tested a meter that shows tutors how much they and their students talk, and found that students talked more. The record does not name Cuemath, and it measured talk, not math learning [3][9].

Tutoring in general has strong evidence. Across 263 randomized trials it averaged 0.40 standard deviations, and 0.16 to 0.22 in large U.S. programs measured on standardized tests [10]. That evidence is about tutoring, not about Cuemath's classes.
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison: worked examples improve math performance across 55 studies [12], and practice that mixes and spaces topics scored 62% against 38% for practice in blocks a month later, in a randomized trial that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations [11]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: You want a live tutor to teach your child, following the school's curriculum.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate test.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your child is at different levels in different parts of math.
You want to see the actual problems behind every number.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Cuemath?
questions.answer: Cuemath teaches in live classes with one tutor, who decides what comes next after a starting evaluation [1][6]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Cuemath work?
questions.answer: We found no study comparing Cuemath students with similar students, and no Cuemath entry in Evidence for ESSA or the What Works Clearinghouse [7][8]. Tutoring in general has strong evidence in randomized trials [10].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
